In a sense, the psychoanalyst likewise develops a maternal ear. This ear becomes attuned to the symbols and acoustic images that matter.

One of the domains I shall address from the psychoanalyst's perspective is entitled "The Necessity of Rewriting the History of Iran for Iranians". On other occasions I shall examine what historiography has been for us Iranians and why it has been distorted—what political hands and what ideological hands have been at work to pull our clear, evident, and lucid history in a particular direction. As the saying goes, everyone has pulled the blanket over to their own side. As soon as we turn to a particular strand of historiography, we see how the blanket has been pulled to their side. The psychoanalyst's task, when casting his gaze upon these written histories, can be to draw out insights from between the lines of these historical writings so as to show where things have been exaggerated, where we ought not to have gone so far regarding historical events, and where justice and respect ought to have been observed. In other words, in *The Psychoanalyst's Gaze* I shall seek to acquaint you with the possibility of deviation from reality. For this reason, we must offer a definition of reality. Reality is what exists, what takes place. That is reality; yet each of us sees and hears this reality in a particular manner. Our film camera views the images, sounds, and readings of what has occurred from its own angle and transforms them into its own truth—meaning that each of us constructs an inner truth from that reality according to the kind of camera at our disposal. Hence, we can never reflect any reality in the complete sense of the word, because we deal with symbols: from every reality, we construct through symbols a truth drawn from the event that took place. We live in this world through our five senses. Our presence in existence is mediated by these five senses and their combination. Our impressions and perceptions of reality reach us through these five senses; we name these perceptions, and by naming them we even enter into relation in a certain way with our own bodies and with others. Let us therefore not attribute to reality the truth that you and I draw and reflect from a singular reality. That is my truth and your truth. One may say that there is no absolute truth in psychoanalysis. In psychoanalysis, everyone holds their own truth from their own vantage point. Everyone films reality with their own signifiers, their own words, their own signs, archives it, and brings it forth when needed. That is why we see to what extent historical films represent the truth of the screenwriter, the truth of the director, and even the truth of the actors who, when speaking, pause or do not pause, or place stress on a given syllable or do not. In effect, through our bodies reality enters into relation with the symbol (word-making and symbolisation); as a result, we arrive at a truth which we sometimes assume to be absolute, though of course it is not. It is for this reason that when we come to realise that every truth is merely an individual truth, we may become considerably more balanced and practise tolerance towards others; for we have recognised that my truth is not absolute, and the other also holds a truth. We must bring both truths together and see where they converge and where they diverge. It is in this way that we shall examine historiography for Iranians. Later, in one of the instalments, I shall present concrete cases and examples from history in full.

Another domain that I shall examine through the psychoanalyst's gaze is poetry; for, as Freud said, poetry and dreams are two paths—two royal roads—to knowing the unconscious, since neither poetry nor dreams are voluntary. I do not decide by an act of will what dream I shall dream. When I dream a dream, it undoubtedly issues from the productions of my unconscious. Likewise, when I compose poetry, this poetry (especially in the *ghazal*, where there is no insistence that one particular couplet must necessarily follow another) is in fact the poet's very free association, using these words, using these couplets, arranging them side by side in a patterned form with rhyme; and when one couplet follows another, we see that if their order were altered, they might no longer convey the meaning intended by the poet. Thus, one may say that here lies another site where the psychoanalyst can hear another inner truth: in dreams and in poetry.

Another domain where the psychoanalyst's gaze may intervene encompasses all human productions, such as drama, cinema, film, song, fable, story, and speech—especially if it is an unscripted speech delivered in a state of emotion, under pressure, when seeking to convey an important message, uttered very freely and spontaneously. The psychoanalyst can scrutinise these productions in detail in order to articulate the psychoanalyst's gaze.

My aim here is not merely to offer various examples. My goal is to provide training so that your ear, too, may become the ear of a psychoanalyst. To put it more simply: the psychoanalyst speaks with his ear, with his ears, with the gravity of the silence of his listening. Let me recount a memory. In the classes I teach over Skype for psychoanalysts inside the country, one day I suggested inviting one of my French patients to hold a question-and-answer session with her—on the condition, however, that we would not enter into what she raised concerning herself personally, but rather ask how she had experienced the stages of her psychoanalysis. This French female patient made a very striking observation. One of my psychiatrist friends on the other end of the Skype line asked her: "How did it come about that you grew interested in your own psychoanalysis and continued with it?"

She replied: "I used to go to the psychoanalysis consulting room twice a week. I saw that the psychoanalyst would sit for long minutes, silent and profound, listening to my ordinary everyday remarks, and then respond—with an extraordinarily deep response. I realised that, for the first time in my life, someone was listening to my words so deeply, with such great silence, such calm, and such close attention. So I became interested and wanted to pursue this further and further, because I had realised that, in my entire life, this was the first time such an ear had existed."

The psychoanalyst speaks with his own ears, and in *The Psychoanalyst's Gaze* I shall strive, gradually and by practising upon topical subjects, to convey this gaze to you so that your ears too may incline somewhat towards silence, and all of our ears together may move away from judgement. First, the psychoanalyst listens in silence, attentively and regularly: his focus is wholly present when he is there. Second, it is without judgement or prejudice: that is, the question of whether I like or dislike hearing what the analysand says does not arise at all, nor does the question of whether I like or dislike listening to the address of an Iranian political official; rather, the point is that I listen to this address and this speech without judgement, paying close attention to what is being said, regardless of whether I feel any fondness for this person or not. It is at this point that I can, with impartiality, discern to some extent the truth that lies behind this discourse. Hence: first, attentive, disciplined, and regular listening; second, listening without prior judgement, without prejudice. These two enable us gradually to distance ourselves from the subject of discussion—that is, to strive to let our own prejudices and our own wishes intrude as little as possible upon what reality is and upon the truth we draw from that reality. Of course, it is almost impossible not to let them intrude at all, for from the very outset I may dislike that singer's voice, dislike this actor's build, say to myself "this person is speaking yet again", or dislike the age of this political official. We arrive beforehand carrying prejudices; yet this cannot be the psychoanalyst's gaze—prejudice must not exist. If it exists, my ear will not be a psychoanalyst's ear. That is why, through varied examples, I shall endeavour to share this method with readers and listeners.
